{{Short description|Classification of formal languages}}
In [[theoretical computer science]] and [[formal language theory]], a [[regular language]] is said to be '''star-free''' if it can be described by a [[regular expression]] constructed from the letters of the [[alphabet (computer science)|alphabet]], the [[empty word]], the [[empty set]] symbol, all [[Set operations (Boolean)|boolean operators]] &ndash; including [[Complement (set theory)|complementation]] &ndash; and [[concatenation]] but no [[Kleene star]].<ref name=Law235>Lawson (2004) p.235</ref> The condition is equivalent to having [[generalized star height]] zero.

It turns out some class of [[Transformer (deep learning)|transformers]] exactly corresponds to star-free languages<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yang |first=Andy |last2=Chiang |first2=David |last3=Angluin |first3=Dana |date=2024-12-16 |title=Masked Hard-Attention Transformers Recognize Exactly the Star-Free Languages |url=https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/13d7f172259b11b230cc5da8768abc5f-Abstract-Conference.html |journal=Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems |language=en |volume=37 |pages=10202–10235 |doi=10.52202/079017-0327}}</ref>. 

== Examples ==
All finite languages are star-free. But no having stars does not mean that we are stuck to finite languages. Indeed, we can use the complementation to build infinite languages. Actually, the language <math>\Sigma^*</math> of ''all'' finite words over an alphabet <math>\Sigma</math> is star-free because it is the complement of the empty set, <math>\Sigma^*=\bar{\emptyset}</math>.

Then, the language of words over the alphabet <math>\{a,\,b\}</math> that do not have consecutive a's can be defined as <math>\overline{\Sigma^* aa \Sigma^*}</math>, first constructing the language of words consisting of <math>aa</math> with an arbitrary prefix and suffix, and then taking its complement, which must be all words which do not contain the substring <math>aa</math>.

An example of a regular language which is not star-free is <math>(aa)^*</math>,<ref name="Salomaa1981">{{cite book|author=Arto Salomaa|title=Jewels of Formal Language Theory|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A-hQAAAAMAAJ|year=1981|publisher=Computer Science Press|isbn=978-0-914894-69-8|page=53}}</ref> i.e. the language of strings consisting of an even number of "a". However, for <math>(ab)^*</math> where <math>a \neq b</math>, the language can be defined as <math>\Sigma^* \setminus (b\Sigma^* \cup \Sigma^*a \cup \Sigma^*aa\Sigma^* \cup \Sigma^*bb\Sigma^* )</math>, taking the set of all words and removing from it words starting with <math>b</math>, ending in <math>a</math> or containing <math>aa</math> or <math>bb</math>. However, when <math>a = b</math>, this definition does not create  <math>(aa)^*</math>.

== Characterisations ==

=== Via aperiod syntact monoids ===
[[Marcel-Paul Schützenberger]] characterized star-free languages as those with [[Aperiodic monoid|aperiodic]] [[syntactic monoid]]s.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Marcel-Paul Schützenberger | author-link=Marcel-Paul Schützenberger | title=On finite monoids having only trivial subgroups | journal=Information and Computation| year=1965| volume=8 | issue=2 | pages=190–194|url=http://igm.univ-mlv.fr/~berstel/Mps/Travaux/A/1965-4TrivialSubgroupsIC.pdf | doi=10.1016/s0019-9958(65)90108-7| doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Law262">Lawson (2004) p.262</ref> Said differently, they are characterised as  languages accepted by some [[aperiodic finite-state automaton]] (known as counter-free languages)<ref>{{cite book | last1=McNaughton | first1=Robert | last2=Papert | first2=Seymour | author2-link=Seymour Papert | others=With an appendix by William Henneman | series=Research Monograph | volume=65 | year=1971 | title=Counter-free Automata | publisher=MIT Press | isbn=0-262-13076-9 | zbl=0232.94024 | url-access=registration | url=https://archive.org/details/CounterFre_00_McNa }}</ref>.

=== Logical characterisation ===
They can also be characterized logically as languages definable in FO[<], the [[first-order logic]] over the natural numbers with the less-than relation<ref>{{cite book | last=Straubing | first=Howard | title=Finite automata, formal logic, and circuit complexity | url=https://archive.org/details/finiteautomatafo0000stra | url-access=registration | series=Progress in Theoretical Computer Science | location=Basel | publisher=Birkhäuser | year=1994 | isbn=3-7643-3719-2 | zbl=0816.68086 | page=[https://archive.org/details/finiteautomatafo0000stra/page/79 79] }}</ref>. First-order variables denote positions in words and < means that a position is strictly before another one. Here are some examples.

* The language <math>\Sigma^*</math>(all words) is captured by the tautology <math>\top</math> (no constraints on the words)
* The language of that have no consecutive a's is defined by the FO[<] formula <math>\forall x \forall y \, \Big( \big( a(x) \land x < y \land \neg \exists z (x < z \land z < y) \big) \implies \neg a(y) \Big)</math> meaning for all positions <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>, if <math>x</math> contains letter <math>a</math> and if <math>y</math> is the position after <math>x</math> (<math>y</math> is after <math>x</math> but there is no positions in between <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>), then there is <math>y</math> does not contain letter <math>a</math>.

They can also be characterized by formulas in [[linear temporal logic]].<ref>{{cite book  | last = Kamp| first=Johan Antony Willem |author-link=Hans Kamp | title = Tense Logic and the Theory of Linear Order| publisher =  University of California at Los Angeles (UCLA) | year=1968}}</ref> Here are some examples.

* Again, The language <math>\Sigma^*</math> is captured by the tautology <math>\top</math>
* The language of that have no consecutive a's is defined by the formula in linear temporal logic <math>G(a \rightarrow X \lnot a)</math> where is the meaning is as follows: always (operator <math>G</math>), if there is letter <math>a</math> then at the next step (operator <math>X</math>) there is no letter <math>a</math>.

== Algorithms ==

=== Membership ===
All star-free languages are in uniform [[AC0|AC<sup>0</sup>]]. More precisely, given a star-free language <math>L</math>, deciding whether a word belongs to <math>L</math> is in uniform AC<sup>0</sup>.

=== Non-emptiness ===
It takes non-elementary time to decide whether a star-free language over two letters is empty. More precisely, the non-emptiness problem of starfree language is defined as follows. 

* Input: a string in the symbols of <math>\{a,\,b\}</math>, empty set, concatenation, union, intersection, and complement.
* Output: Whether this language contains any element.

This problem is [[Decidability (logic)|decidable]], but only in [[Nonelementary problem|nonelementary time]]. As immediate corollaries, it is decidable but nonelementary to decide whether two starfree languages are equal, are disjoint, or contain one another.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Stockmeyer |first=Larry Joseph |title=The complexity of decision problems in automata theory and logic. |date=1974 |degree=PhD |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |url=https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/15540}}</ref>
